# Kotsu

> A Japanese orthopedic surgeon checks what the research actually says about staying strong, mobile and young — muscles, bones, joints, connective tissue, skin and hair.

Author: John Ishiguro, MD — Board-certified orthopedic surgeon, Tokyo. Every article grades its claims A–D (see /method/). No affiliate links, no sponsored content.

## Articles
- [Does keyhole surgery help a worn-out knee? What the sham-surgery trials found](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/knee-arthroscopy-degenerative/): Arthroscopic 'clean-ups' and partial meniscectomy were among the most common knee operations for middle-aged and older adults. A surgeon reads the placebo-controlled trials, the head-to-head trials against exercise therapy, and the meta-analysis of benefits and harms.
- [Should you rest in bed when your back goes out?](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/bed-rest-back-pain/): Bed rest was standard advice for acute low back pain for decades. A surgeon reads the randomised trials and the Cochrane review on resting versus staying active — and what the evidence says to do instead.
- [Can your joints really predict the rain?](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/weather-joint-pain/): Many people with arthritis say they can feel a change in the weather. A surgeon reads the large studies on rain, cold, humidity and air pressure — and what they do and do not show about joint and back pain.
- [Your MRI shows a bulging disc. Is that why your back hurts?](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/disc-bulge-mri-back-pain/): Disc bulges and 'degeneration' are common on the scans of people with no back pain at all. A surgeon reads the evidence on what spine MRI findings do and do not explain — and when a scan helps.
- [Do wedge insoles help knee arthritis? What the placebo-controlled trials found](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/wedge-insoles-knee-arthritis/): Lateral wedge insoles are meant to take load off the inner knee. When trials compared them with plain flat insoles, the pain benefit disappeared. A surgeon reads the evidence on insoles and knee braces.
- [Does creatine cause hair loss? The one study behind the fear — and the trial that tested it](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/creatine-hair-loss/): The creatine-baldness worry traces back to a single 2009 study of rugby players. A surgeon reads it, and the 2025 randomised trial that finally measured hair.
- [Do cold plunges speed muscle recovery? What the meta-analyses show — and the catch for lifters](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/cold-plunge-recovery/): Ice baths are everywhere. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses: cold water eases soreness, does little for strength recovery, and done after every strength session may shrink your gains.
- [Is it too late to build muscle after 60? What the trials show](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/muscle-after-60/): Many people believe lost muscle can't be rebuilt in later life. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses of strength training in adults over 50, over 75 and even over 90.
- [Does vitamin D prevent falls in older adults? What the trials found](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/vitamin-d-falls/): Vitamin D is often recommended to keep older people on their feet. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses of falls trials — and the one trial where a big yearly dose made falls more common.
- [Do calcium supplements prevent fractures? What the trials found](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/calcium-fractures/): Calcium pills are taken by millions of older adults to protect their bones. A surgeon reads the large trials and meta-analyses on calcium, vitamin D and broken bones.
- [Is sitting the new smoking? What the numbers actually show](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/sitting-new-smoking/): Long sitting is linked to a higher risk of death, but the size of that link is far smaller than smoking's, and enough daily activity appeared to cancel it in a study of over a million people.
- [Is weight training bad for older joints? What the trials show](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/strength-training-joints/): Many people over 50 avoid lifting weights to protect their knees. A surgeon reads three large bodies of evidence on strength training, joint pain and safety.
- [Do you really need 10,000 steps a day? What step-counter studies show](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/10000-steps/): The benefits of walking rise steeply up to about 7,000 steps a day and then level off, especially after 60. A surgeon explains what two large analyses found.
- [Does stretching before exercise prevent injuries? Strength training does far more](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/stretching-injury/): A meta-analysis of 25 trials with 26,610 people found no injury-prevention effect from stretching, while strength training cut sports injuries to less than a third. A surgeon explains.
- [Does glucosamine rebuild knee cartilage? What the trials actually measured](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/glucosamine-cartilage/): Glucosamine is sold as a cartilage builder. Large trials that measured the joint space on X-rays found tiny or no differences from placebo. A surgeon explains the numbers.
- [Biotin for hair: does it work, and can it throw off your blood tests?](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/biotin-hair/): Biotin has helped hair only in people with a deficiency or an underlying condition. High doses can also distort lab tests — most often thyroid tests. A surgeon explains.
- [Collagen for joints and skin: what the best trials actually say](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/collagen-skin-joints/): Pooled trials say collagen helps skin, but the independent, high-quality ones don't. For joints, the benefit is short-lived and the evidence weak. A surgeon reads the fine print.
- [Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/knuckle-cracking/): One of the most repeated warnings in medicine has little evidence behind it. What the studies of habitual knuckle crackers found — and what the 'pop' actually is.
- [Does running ruin your knees? What 125,000 people tell us](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/running-knees/): Recreational runners had less hip and knee arthritis than non-runners in a large meta-analysis. Competitive runners had more. A surgeon explains what that does and does not prove.
- [Grip strength: the vital sign hiding in your hand](https://kotsuhealth.com/articles/grip-strength/): Weaker grip goes with shorter life in huge studies across the world. What that does and does not mean, and what you can actually change.
